description: A semi-synthetic penicillinase-resistant isoxazolyl penicillin active against penicillinase-producing staphylococci, used for MSSA skin, soft tissue, and respiratory tract infections.
mechanism_of_action: Binds to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting the transpeptidation step of peptidoglycan synthesis; bulky isoxazolyl side chain prevents degradation by staphylococcal beta-lactamase.
pharmacodynamics: Time-dependent bactericidal action against methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) and Streptococcus species; inactive against MRSA and Enterococcus.
absorption: Incompletely absorbed (approx. 50%); food significantly impairs absorption (take 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals).
distribution: Diffuses into synovial, pleural, and bone fluids; poor CSF penetration in the absence of inflamed meninges; 94% bound to albumin.
metabolism: Partially metabolized in the liver (approx. 20-30%) to active and inactive metabolites.
excretion: Eliminated in urine by tubular secretion and glomerular filtration (approx. 40-60% unchanged); significant biliary excretion.
indications: Infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci (MSSA)
Skin and soft tissue infections (boils, cellulitis, impetigo)
Staphylococcal osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
Infective endocarditis due to MSSA
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to cloxacillin, penicillins, or cephalosporins
History of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction with isoxazolyl penicillins
warnings: Must be taken on an empty stomach to avoid severe absorption loss
Cholestatic jaundice and hepatitis may occur (especially with prolonged therapy)
drug_interactions: Probenecid (blocks renal tubular secretion, increasing cloxacillin levels)
monitoring: Renal function and complete blood count
pregnancy: Category B; widely considered safe in pregnancy when clinically indicated.
lactation: Excreted in low levels in breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Approved in children; dose calculated by weight (50-100 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours).
geriatric: Age-related renal decline requires monitoring; no primary adjustment if hepatic function normal.
renal: Dose reduction needed only in severe renal failure (CrCl < 10 mL/min) due to secondary biliary clearance.
hepatic: Contraindicated in patients with a history of cloxacillin-induced cholestatic jaundice.
advantages: Resistant to staphylococcal penicillinase enzymes (unlike penicillin G or ampicillin)
Effective oral and parenteral option for confirmed MSSA infections
Dual renal and biliary excretion limits toxicity in renal disease
disadvantages: Must be taken on an empty stomach due to severe food-dependent absorption reduction
key_points: First-line for penicillinase-producing staphylococcal skin infections (MSSA)
Always take 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals on an empty stomach
memory_trick: CLOX-acillin: CLOCKS MSSA staph; Check empty stomach.

description: A parenteral penicillinase-resistant isoxazolyl penicillin indicated for severe systemic methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections including bacteremia, endocarditis, and osteomyelitis.
mechanism_of_action: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), causing cell wall weakening and osmotic lysis; stable against staphylococcal beta-lactamases.
pharmacodynamics: Time-dependent bactericidal killing against MSSA and Streptococcus pneumoniae/pyogenes; inactive against MRSA, Enterococci, and Gram-negative bacilli.
absorption: Administered parenterally (IM or IV infusion); 100% bioavailable.
distribution: Distributes into pericardial fluid, bone, and pleural fluid; does not cross non-inflamed meninges; 90-94% bound to plasma albumin.
metabolism: Metabolized partially in the liver to active and inactive metabolites; undergoes substantial biliary excretion.
excretion: Excreted in urine via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion (approx. 40-50%) and in bile (approx. 20-30%).
indications: Severe systemic infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci
MSSA bacteremia and sepsis
MSSA infective endocarditis (standard first-line therapy)
Staphylococcal osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
Complicated skin and skin structure infections
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to oxacillin, penicillins, or other beta-lactams
warnings: Hepatotoxicity: elevated serum transaminases and hepatitis can occur (more frequent than with cefazolin)
drug_interactions: Aminoglycosides (synergistic against MSSA, but must not be mixed in same IV bag)
monitoring: Serum AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase weekly during high-dose therapy
Complete blood count with differential weekly for neutropenia
pregnancy: Category B; safe during pregnancy for severe MSSA infections.
lactation: Excreted in low levels in breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Weight-based dosing in pediatric patients (100-200 mg/kg/day IV divided every 6 hours).
geriatric: Monitor renal and hepatic parameters; adjust based on clinical response.
renal: No dose adjustment required in mild to moderate renal impairment; in severe renal failure with hepatic impairment, reduce dose.
hepatic: Dose reduction and close liver enzyme monitoring required in patients with severe preexisting liver disease.
advantages: First-line gold standard bactericidal agent for MSSA endocarditis and bacteremia
Does not require renal dose adjustments in mild-to-moderate impairment due to biliary elimination
Rapid bacterial clearance in deep MSSA abscesses
disadvantages: High rate of chemical phlebitis requiring dedicated central line or frequent IV site rotation
key_points: Gold standard IV drug for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) bacteremia
Rotate IV sites or use a central line due to risk of vein irritation (phlebitis)
memory_trick: OXA-cillin: Out-maneuvers Staph beta-lactamase; eXcellent for MSSA bacteremia.

description: An ultra-long-acting repository intramuscular penicillin that releases penicillin G over 3 to 4 weeks, serving as the global first-line curative therapy for syphilis and secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever.
dosage_forms: Sterile Suspension for Deep IM Injection
mechanism_of_action: Slowly releases penicillin G from the deep intramuscular depot; penicillin G binds to bacterial PBPs, inhibiting cross-linking of peptidoglycan chains, resulting in bacterial lysis.
pharmacodynamics: Low but sustained bactericidal serum concentrations maintained for 21 to 28 days; exquisitely lethal against Treponema pallidum and Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus).
absorption: Administered exclusively by deep intramuscular injection; extremely slow absorption from depot site over 1 to 4 weeks.
distribution: Distributes into extracellular fluid, placenta, and tissues; does NOT achieve therapeutic levels in the central nervous system (not indicated for neurosyphilis); 60% protein bound.
excretion: Excreted slowly by the kidneys via tubular secretion as active penicillin G over 3 to 4 weeks.
bioavailability: Depot release ensures 100% systemic bio-availability over 3-4 weeks
half_life: Depot elimination half-life is 14 to 30 days
onset: Serum levels detectable within 1 to 2 hours, sustained for 21-28 days
indications: Syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent: single 2.4 MU dose; late latent: 2.4 MU weekly for 3 doses)
Prophylaxis of rheumatic fever (1.2 MU every 3 to 4 weeks)
Streptococcal pharyngitis (single injection treatment)
Yaws and pinta eradication
contraindications: NEVER ADMINISTER INTRAVENOUSLY (causes fatal cardiorespiratory arrest and emboli)
warnings: Black box warning: FOR DEEP INTRAMUSCULAR USE ONLY; inadvertent IV administration causes fatal cardiac arrest and permanent neurovascular damage (Hoigné syndrome / Nicolau syndrome)
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, chills, headache, hypotension) within 24 hours of treating syphilis
Skin allergy testing recommended in suspected allergy
common_adverse_effects: Severe localized pain at intramuscular injection site
serious_adverse_effects: Fatal pulmonary embolism / cardiac arrest if accidentally injected IV
Nicolau syndrome (livedoid dermatitis and tissue necrosis from arterial injection)
drug_interactions: Bacteriostatic antibiotics (tetracyclines - may antagonize bactericidal action)
monitoring: Prior history of penicillin allergy before every dose
Monitor for 30 minutes post-injection for acute anaphylaxis
VDRL / RPR titers at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-syphilis therapy
pregnancy: Category B; drug of choice and ONLY proven curative treatment for syphilis in pregnant women (prevents congenital syphilis).
lactation: Excreted in low levels in breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Single dose of 600,000 units (for children <27 kg) for rheumatic fever prophylaxis and streptococcal tonsillitis.
geriatric: Assess injection site muscle mass; use appropriate needle gauge (18-20G) to prevent depot clogging.
renal: Dosing interval may be extended in severe renal failure, but depot clearance is predominantly slow dissolution.
advantages: Single-dose curative therapy for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis
Monthly deep IM injection guarantees 100% compliance for rheumatic fever prophylaxis
Only therapy proven to prevent congenital syphilis in pregnancy
disadvantages: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED VIA IV: IV injection is immediately fatal
Deep intramuscular injection is painful and causes local muscle tenderness
key_points: CRITICAL SAFETY RULE: For deep INTRAMUSCULAR injection ONLY; NEVER inject IV
Single 2.4 million unit dose cures early syphilis and prevents congenital syphilis in pregnancy
memory_trick: BENZATHINE: Binds to Extracellular Non-vascular muscle; Zero IV allowed (FATAL); Syphilis savior.

description: A natural parenteral penicillin with high intrinsic potency against sensitive streptococci, Neisseria meningitidis, Treponema pallidum (neurosyphilis), and clostridial infections.
mechanism_of_action: Binds to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting transpeptidase enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan polymers in bacterial cell walls, triggering autolysins and osmotic cell death.
pharmacodynamics: Potent concentration-dependent and time-dependent bactericidal activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Treponema pallidum, and Clostridium perfringens.
absorption: Inactivated by gastric acid (oral bioavailability negligible); administered exclusively IV or IM.
distribution: Distributes into synovial, pericardial, and pleural fluids; penetrates inflamed meninges in bacterial meningitis (CSF levels approx. 5-10% of serum); 60% bound to plasma albumin.
metabolism: Metabolized in the liver (approx. 20-30%) to penicilloic acid; minimal CYP involvement.
excretion: Excreted rapidly by the kidneys through active tubular secretion (approx. 90%) and glomerular filtration (approx. 10%).
half_life: 30 to 50 minutes (prolonged in neonates and severe renal failure to 4-10 hours)
indications: Neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis (18 to 24 million units IV daily for 10-14 days)
Meningococcal meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis
Severe streptococcal pneumonia and bacteremia
Infective endocarditis caused by viridans group streptococci (combined with gentamicin)
Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and tetanus (Clostridium tetani)
Actinomycosis
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to penicillin G or any beta-lactam antibiotic
warnings: Electrolyte overload: 1 million units of potassium penicillin contains 1.7 mEq K+; 1 million units of sodium penicillin contains 2.0 mEq Na+ (risk in heart/renal failure)
Neurotoxicity (seizures, encephalopathy, myoclonus) with high doses in renal impairment
serious_adverse_effects: Penicillin-induced encephalopathy / myoclonic seizures (in renal failure)
drug_interactions: Probenecid (blocks tubular secretion, doubling penicillin G serum levels)
Aminoglycosides (synergistic bactericidal action in endocarditis; infuse separately)
monitoring: Serum electrolytes (sodium and potassium) in patients receiving high-dose therapy (>10-20 MU daily)
Renal function (BUN/creatinine) to adjust dosing interval
pregnancy: Category B; drug of choice for neurosyphilis and Group B streptococcal sepsis in pregnancy.
lactation: Excreted in low concentrations in breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Dosed by units/kg/day (100,000 to 250,000 units/kg/day IV divided every 4-6 hours); monitor renal clearance.
geriatric: High risk of neurotoxicity and electrolyte shifts due to decreased GFR; reduce dose and monitor mental status.
renal: Dose reduction mandatory: if CrCl 30-50 mL/min, give full dose q6h; if CrCl 10-30 mL/min, give full dose q8-12h; if CrCl < 10 mL/min, give full dose q12-18h.
hepatic: No primary dosage adjustment required in hepatic disease.
advantages: First-line treatment of choice for neurosyphilis with proven neurological cures
Superb bactericidal potency against Group A/B streptococci and Neisseria meningitidis
Unmatched safety profile outside of allergy
disadvantages: Must be dosed frequently (every 4 hours IV) due to short 30-minute half-life
High electrolyte load in massive doses (potassium or sodium toxicity risk)
key_points: Drug of choice for neurosyphilis (18-24 MU daily continuous IV or divided q4h)
Watch for electrolyte toxicity: massive doses carry high sodium or potassium loads
memory_trick: BENZYL-penicillin: Backbone for Neurosyphilis, Zero oral absorption, Yields seizures if renal clearance drops.

description: A second-generation cephamycin antibiotic with potent anaerobic activity against Bacteroides fragilis, used for surgical prophylaxis and mixed pelvic and intra-abdominal infections.
mechanism_of_action: Binds to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis; 7-alpha-methoxy group on the beta-lactam ring confers extreme stability against beta-lactamases produced by anaerobic bacteria.
pharmacodynamics: Broad bactericidal action against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, Streptococcus, and importantly anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella, and Peptostreptococcus).
distribution: Distributes into peritoneal fluid, pelvic tissues, gallbladder, and skin; poor CSF penetration; 88% bound to plasma proteins.
metabolism: Not significantly metabolized in the liver (approx. 10% converted to a tautomer with similar antibacterial activity).
excretion: Excreted primarily unchanged in urine via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion (approx. 50-80%); remaining eliminated in bile.
half_life: 3 to 4.6 hours (longer than cefoxitin, allowing twice-daily dosing)
indications: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (colorectal surgery, abdominal/vaginal hysterectomy, cesarean section)
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID - combined with doxycycline)
Intra-abdominal infections (peritonitis, diverticulitis, appendicitis)
Gynecological infections (endometritis, pelvic cellulitis)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to cefotetan, cephalosporins, or cephamycins
warnings: Contains an N-methylthiotetrazole (NMTT) side chain: risk of hypoprothrombinemia, coagulopathy, and bleeding (vitamin K deficiency)
Disulfiram-like ethanol reaction with alcohol ingestion (nausea, vomiting, flushing, tachycardia)
serious_adverse_effects: Severe bleeding / coagulopathy due to NMTT-mediated vitamin K inhibition
drug_interactions: Alcohol / ethanol (severe disulfiram-like reaction; avoid alcohol during and for 72 hours post-therapy)
Oral anticoagulants / warfarin (prolonged prothrombin time and major bleeding risk)
monitoring: Prothrombin time (PT/INR) in patients on prolonged courses or with nutritional deficits (supplement with vitamin K)
pregnancy: Category B; used safely for surgical prophylaxis in cesarean section and pelvic procedures.
lactation: Excreted in human milk in low concentrations; use caution during breastfeeding.
pediatric: Safety and efficacy established in children for intra-abdominal infections and prophylaxis (20-40 mg/kg q12h).
geriatric: Dose reduction required if renal clearance is impaired; monitor PT/INR.
renal: Dose adjustment based on CrCl: if CrCl 30-50 mL/min, give usual dose q24h or half dose q12h; if CrCl 10-30 mL/min, give half dose q24h; if CrCl < 10 mL/min, give quarter dose q24h.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment required in hepatic disease.
advantages: Potent anaerobic coverage against Bacteroides fragilis without needing metronidazole
Longer half-life than cefoxitin allows convenient 12-hourly dosing
Single preoperative dose provides reliable coverage for colorectal and pelvic surgeries
disadvantages: NMTT side chain causes hypoprothrombinemia, bleeding, and severe disulfiram reaction with alcohol
High rate of C. difficile colitis
key_points: Covers anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis) for pelvic and abdominal infections
Warn patients to avoid all alcohol (severe disulfiram reaction due to NMTT side chain)
memory_trick: CEFO-TETAN: Cephamycin for Pelvic/Abdominal anaerobes; NMTT side chain causes Bleeding & Hangover.

description: A classical parenteral cephamycin with high beta-lactamase resistance and anaerobic efficacy against Bacteroides fragilis, used for surgical prophylaxis and pelvic inflammatory disease.
mechanism_of_action: Binds to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), causing bacterial cell wall synthesis inhibition; 7-alpha-methoxy group provides extreme resistance to inactivation by Gram-negative and anaerobic beta-lactamases.
pharmacodynamics: Bactericidal against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella), Gram-positive cocci, and anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium species); does NOT contain the NMTT side chain (no hypoprothrombinemia).
absorption: Administered exclusively parenterally (IV or deep IM); 100% bioavailable.
distribution: Widely distributed into pleural, peritoneal, synovial, and ascitic fluids; minimal CSF penetration; 65-80% bound to plasma proteins.
metabolism: Metabolized in small amounts (approx. 2-5%) to inactive descarbamylcefoxitin.
excretion: Excreted rapidly and primarily unchanged in urine via active tubular secretion (approx. 85%) and glomerular filtration.
indications: Surgical prophylaxis in colorectal, appendectomy, gynecological, and clean-contaminated procedures
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID - combined with oral doxycycline as CDC first-line parenteral regimen)
Intra-abdominal infections (peritonitis, intra-abdominal abscesses)
Diabetic foot infections involving mixed aerobes and anaerobes
warnings: Short half-life necessitates intraoperative redosing for surgical procedures lasting >2-3 hours
Induces chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamases in Enterobacter species (avoid in Enterobacter infections)
drug_interactions: Probenecid (significantly blocks tubular secretion, increasing serum cefoxitin levels)
monitoring: Complete blood count with differential in courses >10 days
Inspection of peripheral IV sites for phlebitis
pregnancy: Category B; first-line CDC-recommended parenteral regimen for pelvic inflammatory disease in pregnancy.
lactation: Excreted in low levels in breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Approved in children 3 months and older (80-160 mg/kg/day divided every 4-6 hours).
geriatric: Renal function declines with age; adjust dose and interval accordingly.
renal: Dose reduction required: if CrCl 30-50 mL/min, give 1-2 g q8-12h; if CrCl 10-29 mL/min, give 1-2 g q12-24h; if CrCl < 10 mL/min, give 0.5-1 g q24-48h.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment required in hepatic impairment.
advantages: First-line CDC-recommended parenteral regimen for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
Does NOT contain the NMTT side chain (no bleeding or disulfiram reaction, unlike cefotetan)
Excellent anaerobic coverage for abdominal and gynecological surgery
disadvantages: Short half-life requires dosing every 6 to 8 hours (or intraoperative redosing during long surgeries)
Strong inducer of AmpC beta-lactamases in Enterobacter, Serratia, and Citrobacter
key_points: CDC first-line inpatient treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID + doxycycline)
Safe anaerobic coverage without bleeding complications because it lacks the NMTT ring
memory_trick: CEFOX-itin: Classic Emergency Cephamycin for Female pelvic inflammatory disease (PID); No NMTT.
